t: Most Expensive Item That Can Not Be Bought
o: With unlimited coins of two coprime denominations a and b, the Frobenius/Chicken McNugget theorem states the largest non-representable amount is a·b − a − b. Example: 2 and 5 give 10−2−5 = 3; 5 and 7 give 35−12 = 23.
k: Chicken McNugget theorem: for coprime a, b the Frobenius number is ab − a − b.
Two distinct primes are always coprime, so the formula applies directly.

a.i: Directly apply the theorem. Every integer above ab−a−b is representable as ax+by with x,y ≥ 0, and ab−a−b itself is not (standard residue argument: multiples of a mod b cycle through all residues, and the last unreachable one is a(b−1) ≡ −a mod b).

To avoid relying on memorized theory, compute reachability bottom-up: x is buyable iff x−a or x−b is buyable. Sweep up to a·b (beyond the Frobenius number everything is reachable) and return the largest unreachable value found. This doubles as a proof-by-construction in an interview.
s: For x from 1 to a*b: dp[x] = (x≥a && dp[x−a]) || (x≥b && dp[x−b]).
Return the largest x with dp[x] false.
a.t: O(a·b) — sieve up to the product (bounded by 10^5 per constraints)

w: Know the formula cold, but be ready to derive or verify it with the DP if asked. Pitfall: the theorem requires coprimality — true for distinct primes here, but state it explicitly. Follow-up: three denominations have no closed form; the DP/sieve generalizes.
